A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same WorldScore benchmark and contain readable main text, equations, tables, figures, and complete supplementary material. Content can be matched across appendix reorganization without material comparison gaps.

before.justification: v1 reports original evaluations of 19 generation models, subdomain analyses, and a human-preference study comparing subjective-quality metrics.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results, evaluates LTX-Video, and adds human-preference validation of additional metrics and a resolution/aspect-ratio robustness experiment.

M1.justification: The world-specification procedure, model-specific input adaptation, ten metrics, normalization, and score aggregation remain unchanged. The selected CLIP-IQA+ and CLIP Aesthetic ensemble is also unchanged; expanded validation does not introduce a new method component.

E1.justification: Both versions use the same 3,000-example benchmark, scene and motion categories, visual styles, and short/long generation tasks. The new validation experiments reuse generated videos and alter comparisons or preprocessing rather than introducing another dataset, domain, or generation task.

E2.justification: Table 2 adds LTX-Video to the evaluated models, increasing the total from 19 to 20 while retaining every previous model. The subjective-quality comparator set in Table S5 remains unchanged.

E3.justification: The reported human-study size changes from 200 to 400 participants. Appendix D adds comparisons between score buckets of 30±5, 60±5, and 90±5, plus an EasyAnimate test comparing native 1344×768 videos with center-cropped/resized 256×256 versions. These are focused protocol additions; the PDFs do not establish which existing results were recomputed.

E4.justification: Validation expands substantially beyond selecting a subjective-quality ensemble. New Table S6 tests human agreement for camera controllability, object controllability, 3D consistency, photometric consistency, and motion magnitude; Table S7 tests sensitivity to resolution and aspect ratio. These directly examine the validity and robustness of the benchmark's measurements.

E5.justification: The probabilistic human-agreement calculation is retained, and neither version reports new repeated-run statistics, seeds, confidence intervals, or significance tests. The increased participant count concerns sample size; the new ±5 notation defines score buckets rather than uncertainty intervals.

E6.justification: Table 2 adds LTX-Video scores of 55.44 for WorldScore-Static and 56.54 for WorldScore-Dynamic; all original 19 model rows remain numerically unchanged. Tables S6–S7 add agreement rates of 71.2–97.3% and resolution-test results. Table S5 remains unchanged. Table S7's largest absolute difference is 0.86, despite the text claiming at most 0.83.

T1.justification: The world-generation formulation, metric definitions, equations S1–S8, empirical-bound construction, and human-agreement definition are unchanged. Moving the agreement definition into Appendix D adds no new mathematical reasoning or proof.

C1.justification: The abstract and introduction expand the claimed evaluation from 19 to 20 models, including 18 rather than 17 open-source models. The central contributions—a unified benchmark, curated dataset, ten metrics, and findings about generation challenges—retain their meaning and scope.

C2.justification: Section 4 and Appendix D newly interpret the validation results as evidence that WorldScore metrics align with human preferences and tolerate resolution/aspect-ratio differences. Existing explanations of model weaknesses and motion tradeoffs remain substantially unchanged.

D1.justification: Table S1 adds LTX-Video's version, 768×512 resolution, four-second duration, 30 FPS, and average generation time of 2.4 minutes. Appendix D documents score-bucket selection and the cropping/resizing validation procedure. Existing hardware and dataset/code access information remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds the LTX-Video reference, removes Ji et al.'s T2VBench reference, and shortens the discussion of specific 4D-generation approaches. The broader positioning against single-scene video benchmarks remains unchanged.

P1.justification: Edits are localized: photometric-consistency and conclusion wording are tightened, a validation paragraph is added, and human-study material moves from Appendix C.4 into an expanded Appendix D. Further Visualization becomes Appendix E, and acknowledgments expand. Most prose and the main narrative structure are retained.

P2.justification: v2 adds Tables S6–S7, inserts LTX-Video rows into Tables 2 and S1, reorders some Table 2 rows, and expands captions. Table S5 and Figure 4 are relocated within the layout. Existing figures and their substantive visual content are retained.

improvement.justification: Compared with v1's validation focused on subjective quality, v2 supplies useful human-agreement evidence for five additional metrics and a controlled resolution/aspect-ratio check, strengthening support for the benchmark. LTX-Video modestly broadens comparison coverage. The gain remains limited by unspecified validation pair/sample counts, robustness testing on one model, and the discrepancy between Table S7's 0.86 maximum change and the claimed 0.83 bound. The core benchmark and previous results remain stable.
